chunks: "High torque corresponds to high current, and high RPM corresponds to high voltage. Why current: torque comes from the Lorentz force on the winding.
Each conductor in the magnetic field feels a force B I , so the total torque is proportional to current, T equals K tI .
To get more torque I have to push more current through the winding. That's why a stalled motor, which is making maximum torque, draws maximum current, V over R .
Why voltage for speed: when the rotor spins, the same conductors cutting the field generate a back-EMF, E equals K e omega , which opposes the supply.
The motor settles at the speed where that back-EMF is nearly equal to the applied voltage.
The voltage equation is V equals IR plus K e omega , so omega equals (V minus IR) over K e : speed is roughly proportional to voltage, minus a drop that grows with load current.
The two constants are actually the same number in SI units: K t in N·m per amp equals K e in volt-seconds per radian.
You can prove it with energy conservation: the electrical power converted, EI equals K e omega I , must equal the mechanical power T omega equals K tI omega .
In practice, this means current-limiting a driver limits torque, and PWM duty sets speed.
And a heavier load pulls the speed down a bit because it needs more current, which means a bigger IR drop."
